Tolstoy exposes the hypocrisy of a society that forgives men and punishes women, and the cruelty with which it enforces its rules.

Levin's questions about death, faith and purpose run through the novel, alongside the farm reforms and political debates of 1870s Russia. Tolstoy contrasts Anna's final ride, seeing only hatred everywhere, with Levin's realization that goodness gives life meaning. Both face despair; one finds a reason to live, rooted in simple love and work.

cards.t: Build love on more than excitement
cards.b: Anna and Vronsky's romance began with a thrilling dance and a snowy station; it ended in suspicion and despair. Intense feelings are wonderful, but they need a shared life to rest on. In any relationship, look for what you are building together, not just how it makes you feel at its most exciting.

cards.t: Don't keep up appearances at all costs
cards.b: Karenin wanted Anna to stay home and pretend all was well, protecting his reputation while his marriage rotted. Choosing how things look over how they are rarely solves anything. When something is broken in your home or work, address the real problem, even if it is embarrassing.

cards.t: Find meaning in work you can touch
cards.b: Levin found joy mowing hay with the peasants, losing himself in honest physical work. Purpose often comes not from abstract arguments but from doing something useful with your hands and attention. When life feels empty, try a task that absorbs you fully, whether gardening, cooking, building or caring for someone.

Levin dreaded his dying brother's bedside, but Kitty went and nursed Nikolai with practical tenderness. Showing up for people in illness and grief is frightening, and we often fear doing it wrong. Go anyway. Your presence and small acts of care matter more than knowing the right words.

Anna's jealousy grew with every absence of Vronsky's, until she read betrayal into the smallest note. Suspicion can create the very distance it fears. When jealousy rises, name the fear behind it and talk about it directly, rather than letting it harden into accusations and resentment.

Society's cruelty to Anna at the opera contributed to her isolation and despair, while Dolly, visiting her, was moved to compassion. Before condemning someone whose choices you disapprove of, remember how little you know of their struggle. Kindness can be a lifeline for someone on the edge.

cards.t: Goodness is enough to live by
cards.b: Levin did not solve every theological question; he simply realized that living for goodness and for others gave his life meaning. You do not need all the answers before you begin. Choose to do good in the small, specific ways in front of you, and meaning can grow from there.

Tolstoy says every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way. Think of a relationship in your life that has felt strained. What is its particular kind of unhappiness, and what is one small step, like Kitty's chalk letters, that might open a new conversation?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: You cannot buy back the past
pts.d: Gatsby builds a fortune and a mansion to win Daisy as she was in 1917, and fails.

pts.h: Old money protects itself
pts.d: Tom and Daisy smash up things and people, then retreat into their wealth and let others pay.

pts.h: The American Dream can become an illusion
pts.d: the green light across the bay promises a future that keeps receding.

pts.h: Reinvention has limits
pts.d: James Gatz from North Dakota becomes Jay Gatsby, but cannot escape where he came from.

cards.b: In the summer of 1922, the height of the Jazz Age and Prohibition, Nick Carraway, a Yale-educated young man from the Midwest, moves east to learn the bond business in New York. He rents a small cottage in West Egg, a Long Island village of new money, beside a gigantic mansion owned by a mysterious man named Gatsby. Across the bay, in fashionable, old-money East Egg, live Nick's cousin Daisy and her husband Tom Buchanan, a hugely rich former Yale football star. One evening Nick sees Gatsby alone on his lawn, stretching his arms toward a green light across the water.

At dinner with Tom and Daisy, Nick meets Daisy's friend Jordan Baker, a cool, bored professional golfer. Tom is arrogant and brutish, ranting about a racist book claiming the white race will be swamped. A phone call interrupts the meal, and Jordan explains that Tom has a woman in New York. Daisy, charming and restless, tells Nick she hopes her baby daughter will be a beautiful little fool, because that is the best thing a girl can be in this world. Nick senses that the Buchanans' glittering life hides deep unhappiness and carelessness.

Between West Egg and New York lies the valley of ashes, a grey wasteland of coal dust overlooked by a faded billboard showing the giant spectacled eyes of an oculist, Doctor T. J. Eckleburg. There Tom takes Nick to a garage run by George Wilson, a weary, spiritless man whose wife, Myrtle, is Tom's mistress. Tom, Myrtle and Nick go to an apartment in New York for a drunken party. When Myrtle insists on her right to say Daisy's name, Tom breaks her nose with a single blow of his open hand.

Every weekend Gatsby throws enormous parties. Cars ferry guests from the city, orchestras play, and crates of oranges and lemons arrive and leave as pulp. Most guests are never invited; they simply come, and they gossip about their host: he killed a man, he was a German spy, he went to Oxford. Nick, who receives a formal invitation, finally meets Gatsby, a young man with a radiant, understanding smile and an elaborate way of speaking, who calls everyone 'old sport'. Gatsby seems oddly detached from his own parties.

Gatsby drives Nick to the city, telling him he is the son of wealthy Midwestern people, educated at Oxford, and decorated for bravery in the war. Over lunch Nick meets Gatsby's associate Meyer Wolfsheim, a gangster said to have fixed the 1919 World Series. Then Jordan tells Nick the real secret. In 1917 in Louisville, Daisy, the most popular girl in town, fell in love with a young officer named Jay Gatsby. He went to war, and she married Tom. Gatsby bought his mansion to be across the bay from her, and he wants Nick to invite Daisy to tea.

On a rainy afternoon, Daisy comes to Nick's cottage, and Gatsby arrives so nervous that he almost knocks over a clock. After a painfully awkward start, Nick leaves them alone, and when he returns Daisy has been crying and Gatsby glows with happiness. Gatsby shows them his mansion and its treasures. He tosses heaps of beautiful shirts on the bed, and Daisy sobs into them. Nick notices that the green light at the end of Daisy's dock, which once seemed to hold all Gatsby's dreams, is now just a light on a dock.

Nick later learns Gatsby's true history. He was born James Gatz to poor farmers in North Dakota and invented a new self at seventeen, when he rowed out to warn the millionaire Dan Cody's yacht of a storm. Cody hired him and taught him the ways of the rich, but Gatz never received the inheritance. Now Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby's parties. Tom sneers, and Daisy is offended by the vulgarity of West Egg. Gatsby tells Nick he wants Daisy to say she never loved Tom, so they can start over as if five years had never passed.

cards.q: Can't repeat the past? Why of course you can!
cards.b: Gatsby's incredulous reply to Nick, from the novel now in the public domain, is the turning point. Everything he has done has been to recover a single moment in 1917. Nick sees the danger: Gatsby wants not just Daisy's love, but the erasure of time itself.

On a stifling hot day, the Buchanans, Gatsby, Nick and Jordan drive into New York and take a suite at the Plaza Hotel. Gatsby's mention that Daisy's voice is full of money says much about what he loves. Tom confronts Gatsby, mocking him as Mr. Nobody from Nowhere and revealing that he made his fortune bootlegging alcohol through drugstores. Gatsby insists that Daisy never loved Tom. Daisy cannot say it; she admits she loved them both. As Tom presses on, Gatsby's dream visibly dies, and Daisy draws away from him.

Tom sends Daisy home with Gatsby in Gatsby's yellow car. In the valley of ashes, Myrtle Wilson, whom her suspicious husband had locked up after discovering her affair, breaks free and runs into the road, thinking the car is Tom's. The car hits her and kills her, and does not stop. Tom, Nick and Jordan, driving behind, see the crowd and the body. Back at East Egg, Nick finds Gatsby hiding in the bushes. Gatsby admits that Daisy was driving, but says he will take the blame.

Gatsby keeps watch outside the Buchanans' house all night in case Tom hurts Daisy. Nick looks through a window and sees Tom and Daisy at the kitchen table over cold fried chicken and ale, talking intimately, as if conspiring. The next morning Gatsby tells Nick the whole story of his love for Daisy in Louisville. As Nick leaves, he calls back across the lawn that Gatsby is worth the whole rotten bunch put together. Gatsby smiles. It is the only compliment Nick ever gives him.

George Wilson, crazed with grief and convinced that the driver of the yellow car was his wife's lover, walks across Long Island. Tom tells him that the car belonged to Gatsby. That afternoon Gatsby goes for a swim in his pool for the first time that summer, still waiting for a call from Daisy. Wilson finds him floating on an air mattress and shoots him dead, then turns the gun on himself. The newspapers tell a garbled story. Daisy and Tom quietly leave town, leaving no forwarding address.

Nick tries to gather mourners. The hundreds who drank Gatsby's champagne do not come. Wolfsheim refuses, saying friendship is for a man while he is alive. Only Gatsby's father, Henry Gatz, arrives from Minnesota, proudly showing Nick a boyhood schedule in which young Jimmy planned exercise, study and self-improvement. In the rain, the only other mourner is an owl-eyed man who once admired Gatsby's library. Nick ends his affair with Jordan, and when he meets Tom on Fifth Avenue, Tom admits he sent Wilson to Gatsby and feels he was justified.

Disgusted with the East, Nick decides to return to the Midwest. He concludes that Tom and Daisy were careless people: they smashed up things and people, then retreated into their money and let others clean up their mess. On his last night, he sits on Gatsby's beach thinking of the Dutch sailors who first saw this fresh green island, and of Gatsby's belief in the green light, the future that recedes before us. We keep reaching for it anyway, Nick reflects, like boats rowing against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.

Gatsby is a bootlegger, a liar and a self-invented man, yet Nick calls him great. What makes him great is his extraordinary gift for hope and his total devotion to a dream. He believes he can remake himself and reverse time through will and money. His tragedy is that the dream was always bigger than the woman.

Daisy is charming, beautiful and her voice is full of money. She once truly loved Gatsby, but she chose security and status with Tom. Fitzgerald presents her as both victim and accomplice: trapped in a careless marriage, yet unwilling to give up its comforts. She lets Gatsby take the blame and leaves without a word.

Nick claims he is slow to judge, but he narrates with growing disgust. Drawn into the glamour of the East, he becomes Gatsby's only friend and the moral voice of the book. He is not innocent: he helps arrange the affair and drifts with Jordan. His final decision to go home is a rejection of the whole careless world.

Gatsby's rise from a poor farm boy to a millionaire embodies the American belief that anyone can remake themselves. But his fortune comes from crime, and old money never accepts him. Fitzgerald suggests the dream has become corrupted by materialism, and that its promise, like the green light, always remains just out of reach.

East Egg's old money, West Egg's new money and the valley of ashes form a map of American class. Tom and Daisy can afford to be careless because their wealth protects them; Myrtle, George and Gatsby pay with their lives. The novel exposes how privilege shields the rich from the consequences of their actions.

Gatsby believes he can repeat the past, and he arranges his whole life around a single month in Louisville. Clocks, seasons and memories run through the novel, from the clock Gatsby nearly knocks over to the final image of boats borne back into the past. Fitzgerald suggests that longing for a lost moment can make the present impossible to live.

cards.t: Love the person, not the memory
cards.b: Gatsby loved the Daisy of 1917 and could not accept the real woman, a wife and mother, in front of him. Clinging to an idealized memory of someone can blind us to who they are now. In old friendships and relationships, try to meet people as they are today, not as you remember them.

Hundreds came to Gatsby's parties; almost no one came to his funeral. Popularity is not the same as friendship. Notice who shows up when there is nothing to gain, as Nick did, and make sure you are that kind of friend to someone else.

Tom and Daisy smashed up lives and retreated into their money. Most of us are not rich enough to escape consequences, but we can still be careless, with promises, with others' feelings, with our words. Take responsibility for the damage you cause, even when you could get away with it.

Young Jimmy Gatz's schedule of self-improvement was admirable; building a new identity on lies and crime was not. You are allowed to grow beyond where you came from. Do it through real effort and honesty, and you will not live in fear that someone like Tom will expose you.

Nick told Gatsby he was worth the whole bunch put together, and was glad he said it, because it was the last time they spoke. If you admire or appreciate someone, tell them. We rarely know which conversation will be our last chance to say it.

Gatsby's mansion, shirts and parties could not make Tom accept him or win back Daisy's past. Money can buy comfort and attention, but not respect, love or the past. Before chasing something to impress others, ask whether it will actually bring you the connection you want.

cards.t: Leave a world that corrupts you
cards.b: After Gatsby's death Nick saw the East's glamour for what it was and went home. Sometimes the healthiest choice is to walk away from a setting, a job, a social circle, a city, that is making you careless or cynical. Choosing your environment is part of choosing who you become.

Gatsby kept reaching for a green light across the bay. What is your green light, the dream that seems always a little out of reach? Is it a real future you are building toward, or a past moment you are trying to repeat?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Ambition without conscience destroys itself
pts.d: Macbeth kills a king for the crown and ends up friendless, hated and despairing.

pts.h: One crime leads to the next
pts.d: after Duncan come the grooms, Banquo, and Macduff's wife and children.

pts.h: Guilt cannot be washed away
pts.d: Lady Macbeth, once so steely, sleepwalks scrubbing blood only she can see.

pts.h: Prophecy tempts but does not compel
pts.d: the witches never tell Macbeth to murder; his own desire fills in the rest.

cards.b: In medieval Scotland, the gentle old King Duncan faces a rebellion and an invasion from Norway. His general Macbeth, Thane of Glamis, wins a ferocious victory alongside his friend Banquo. Riding home across a bleak heath in thunder, the two men meet three weird sisters, bearded witches who hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and king hereafter. To Banquo they promise that, though he will not be king, his descendants will be. Then the witches vanish into the air, leaving both men startled and Macbeth strangely shaken.

Moments later, the nobles Ross and Angus arrive with news: Duncan has executed the traitorous Thane of Cawdor and given his title to Macbeth. The first prophecy has come true. Macbeth begins to imagine murdering Duncan, and the thought terrifies him. At court, Duncan thanks him warmly, but then names his elder son Malcolm as heir, the Prince of Cumberland, a step in Macbeth's way. Duncan announces that he will honor Macbeth by staying the night at his castle at Inverness. Macbeth sends a letter ahead to his wife.

Lady Macbeth reads the letter and immediately resolves that her husband shall be king. She fears he is too full of the milk of human kindness to seize the crown, and she calls on dark spirits to fill her with cruelty. When Macbeth arrives, she tells him Duncan must never see tomorrow's sun. Macbeth wavers: Duncan is his king, his kinsman and his guest, and a good ruler. Lady Macbeth taunts his courage and manhood and lays out a plan to drug Duncan's guards and blame them. Macbeth agrees.

That night, waiting for his wife's signal, Macbeth sees a vision of a bloody dagger floating before him, pointing toward Duncan's room. He goes in and murders the sleeping king. He returns shattered, still holding the bloody daggers. He heard a voice cry that Macbeth has murdered sleep, and he could not say 'Amen' when a guard prayed. Lady Macbeth scolds him, takes the daggers back and smears the drugged guards with blood. A loud knocking at the gate begins. A drunken porter, joking that he is the gatekeeper of hell, finally opens it.

The knocker is the nobleman Macduff, come to wake the king. He discovers Duncan's body and raises the alarm. Macbeth, claiming fury, kills the two guards before they can speak, and Lady Macbeth faints, or pretends to. Duncan's sons, Malcolm and Donalbain, suspect treachery and flee, Malcolm to England and Donalbain to Ireland, which makes them look guilty. Macbeth is crowned king at Scone. Macduff pointedly does not attend the coronation, and Banquo, remembering the witches, begins to suspect that Macbeth played foully for the crown.

As king, Macbeth is not at peace. He fears Banquo's wisdom and the prophecy that Banquo's sons will reign, meaning that he has murdered Duncan only to put Banquo's line on the throne. He hires murderers to kill Banquo and his young son Fleance as they ride to a royal banquet, and he no longer tells his wife his plans. The murderers ambush them at dusk. Banquo is killed, crying to his son to flee, and Fleance escapes into the darkness. Macbeth's fears are not ended, only renewed.

At the feast, a murderer reports that Banquo is dead but Fleance has escaped. When Macbeth turns to take his seat, he sees Banquo's bloody ghost sitting in his place. No one else can see it. Macbeth raves at the empty chair, and his guests stare in horror. Lady Macbeth tries to cover for him, explaining that he has suffered fits since his youth, and finally sends everyone away. Alone with her, Macbeth reflects that blood will have blood, and resolves to visit the witches again to learn the worst.

cards.q: I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more, / Returning were as tedious as go o'er.
cards.b: Macbeth's words after the banquet are the play's turning point. He is waist-deep in a river of blood, and going back seems as hard as going on. From here he stops hesitating and kills freely; his conscience has not vanished, but he has decided to ignore it.

In a cave, around a boiling cauldron, the witches summon apparitions. An armed head warns him to beware Macduff. A bloody child tells him no man born of woman shall harm him. A crowned child holding a tree says he will never be defeated until Great Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane Hill. Macbeth feels invincible, yet he is shown a procession of eight kings descended from Banquo. Learning that Macduff has fled to England, Macbeth orders his castle seized, and Lady Macduff and all her children are slaughtered.

In England, Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty by pretending to be even more lustful and greedy than Macbeth. When Macduff despairs for Scotland, Malcolm reveals that it was a test and that he is ready to fight, with English troops. Then Ross arrives with terrible news: Macduff's wife, children and servants have all been murdered. Macduff is stunned, asking whether all his pretty chickens and their mother were killed at one fell swoop. Urged to dispute it like a man, he says he must also feel it as a man. Grief turns to resolve.

At Dunsinane, a doctor and a gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth walk in her sleep, carrying a candle, because she now insists on having light by her always. She rubs her hands as if washing them and murmurs about a damned spot of blood that will not come out, about Duncan, about Lady Macduff, and about a smell of blood that all the perfumes of Arabia cannot sweeten. The woman who once said a little water would clear them of the deed now cannot stop washing. The doctor says she needs a priest more than a physician.

As English and Scottish forces approach, Macbeth's thanes desert him. Malcolm orders each soldier to cut a branch from Birnam Wood and carry it to hide their numbers. A cry of women is heard: Lady Macbeth is dead, apparently by her own hand. Macbeth responds with numb despair, reflecting that life is a walking shadow, a poor player, a tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. Then a messenger reports that Birnam Wood appears to be moving toward Dunsinane. Macbeth realizes the witches have equivocated, but arms himself to fight.

In battle Macbeth kills young Siward, son of the English general, and boasts that no man born of woman can harm him. Then he meets Macduff, who tells him he was from his mother's womb untimely ripped, delivered by cutting before he could be born naturally. Macbeth's courage falters, and he refuses to fight. Macduff threatens to display him as a tyrant in a cage. Rather than yield to Malcolm, Macbeth fights on and is killed. Macduff brings his severed head to Malcolm, who is hailed King of Scotland and invites all to his coronation at Scone.

Macbeth begins as Scotland's greatest soldier, loyal and admired, with a vivid imagination and a sensitive conscience. Ambition, prophecy and his wife's urging overcome his scruples. Each murder deadens him further, until he feels nothing at his wife's death. Shakespeare makes us watch a good man choose evil and lose himself step by step.

Lady Macbeth seems stronger and more ruthless than her husband: she plans the murder, mocks his fear and calmly cleans up. But she has suppressed her own humanity, and it returns as guilt. Excluded from Macbeth's later crimes, she collapses into sleepwalking and death. Her arc mirrors his: he grows harder as she breaks.

Banquo heard the same prophecy but did not act on it, and his line is promised the throne. Macduff loses everything to Macbeth's tyranny, grieves openly and then leads justice. Both offer contrasts to Macbeth: they show that temptation and suffering do not have to lead to crime, and that courage can serve conscience.

Macbeth's vaulting ambition, as he calls it, overleaps itself. The crown brings him no joy, only fear, sleeplessness and isolation. Shakespeare shows ambition untethered from morality turning into tyranny, and every new act of violence becoming necessary to protect the last. The play is a study of how far a person will go once the first line is crossed.

The witches predict, but never instruct; Banquo hears the same words and does nothing. Their later prophecies trick Macbeth with double meanings that only feed his overconfidence. Shakespeare leaves open how much was fated, but he makes clear that Macbeth chooses each murder. Prophecy only gives his desire a shape.

Blood stains every scene: on daggers, hands, ghosts and imagined spots. Sleep becomes the opposite, a symbol of innocence and peace that Macbeth has murdered. Guilt appears as hallucination, insomnia and madness. Shakespeare suggests that crime damages the mind of the criminal, and that no water can wash it away.

cards.t: Notice what a prophecy awakens in you
cards.b: The witches only said 'king hereafter'; it was Macbeth who thought of murder. When someone praises you, predicts your success or flatters your ambitions, pay attention to what it stirs. Ask whether you are being shown a possibility, or being tempted to take a shortcut you would never have considered.

cards.t: Don't let others shame you into wrong
cards.b: Macbeth hesitated until his wife mocked his courage and manhood. Many bad decisions come from not wanting to look weak. If someone tells you that refusing would make you a coward, take that as a warning sign. Real courage sometimes means saying no and enduring the scorn.

After Duncan, Macbeth felt he was too deep in blood to turn back. Wrongdoing often feels easier to continue than to admit. If you realize you have taken a wrong turn, at work, in a relationship or with money, stop at once. Going back may be painful, but going further is usually worse.

cards.t: Guilt needs to be faced, not hidden
cards.b: Lady Macbeth pushed her conscience down until it erupted in her sleep. Unacknowledged guilt rarely disappears; it seeps out as anxiety, insomnia or self-destruction. If something is troubling your conscience, talk about it, make amends where you can, and stop trying to wash away a spot that needs confession.

cards.t: Read the fine print of promises
cards.b: Macbeth trusted that no man born of woman could harm him and that forests do not move, and the witches' tricky wording destroyed him. When a deal, forecast or promise sounds too good to be true, look for the hidden conditions. Overconfidence built on ambiguous assurances is dangerous.

When told to dispute his loss like a man, Macduff answered that he must also feel it as a man. Grief is not weakness. Allowing yourself to feel loss deeply, rather than burying it, gives you the clarity and strength to act, as Macduff did when he finally confronted Macbeth.

By the end, Macbeth's thanes had abandoned him, and he had no friends, honor or love left. He had the crown but nothing that makes life worth living. Whatever position you hold or seek, remember that respect, loyalty and honest relationships are worth far more than the title.

Macbeth's first crime made the next ones feel necessary. Is there a small compromise you made, a shortcut or a half-truth, that is now asking for more to protect it? What would it take to stop wading and turn back today?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Change the scale and folly becomes visible
pts.d: tiny Lilliputians go to war over which end to crack an egg.

pts.h: Pride looks absurd from outside
pts.d: the giant King of Brobdingnag hears Gulliver boast of England and calls humans odious vermin.

pts.h: Reason detached from life is useless
pts.d: Laputa's scholars extract sunbeams from cucumbers while their land starves.

pts.h: Hating humanity is its own madness
pts.d: Gulliver worships the rational horses so much that he can no longer bear his own family.

cards.b: Lemuel Gulliver, an English ship's surgeon with a restless love of travel, sets out on a voyage to the South Seas in 1699. A storm wrecks the ship, and he swims ashore, exhausted, and falls asleep on the grass. He wakes to find himself unable to move: hundreds of fine threads tie him to the ground, and tiny people, less than six inches tall, swarm over his body, shooting needle-like arrows at him. He is in Lilliput. The Lilliputians feed him barrels of wine, haul him on a huge cart to their capital and chain him in an old temple.

Gulliver learns the language and wins the Emperor's favor with gentle behavior. He discovers Lilliput's absurd politics. Officials win high office by dancing on a tightrope before the Emperor. The two political parties, the High-Heels and the Low-Heels, are divided by the height of their shoe heels. Lilliput is also at war with the neighboring island of Blefuscu over a religious dispute: whether boiled eggs should be broken at the big end or the little end. Thousands have died over this question. Swift is mocking English party politics and the bloody quarrels between Catholics and Protestants.

Gulliver wades across the channel and drags away Blefuscu's entire fleet with ropes and hooks, becoming a hero. But when the Emperor asks him to help conquer Blefuscu completely and enslave its people, Gulliver refuses, and he falls out of favor. When a fire breaks out in the Empress's palace, he puts it out by urinating on it, which offends the Empress deeply. His enemies draw up charges of treason, and the 'merciful' sentence is that he will be blinded and slowly starved. Warned by a friend, he flees to Blefuscu, finds a full-sized boat and sails home.

On his second voyage, Gulliver is left behind on an unknown shore and finds himself in Brobdingnag, a land of giants as tall as church steeples, where he is now the tiny one. A farmer finds him in a field and shows him at markets as a curiosity, nearly working him to death. The farmer's nine-year-old daughter, Glumdalclitch, becomes his tender nurse and teacher. Gulliver is sold to the Queen, who adores him, but he is in constant danger: the Queen's spiteful dwarf drops him in a bowl of cream, wasps as big as birds attack him, and a monkey carries him onto a roof.

The wise and kindly King of Brobdingnag questions Gulliver about England. Gulliver proudly describes its Parliament, courts, wars and history. But the King asks searching questions about bribery, corruption, debts and lawyers, and he concludes that European history is a heap of conspiracies, rebellions, murders and massacres. Then Gulliver offers to teach him how to make gunpowder and cannons that could destroy his enemies. The King is horrified and forbids him ever to mention it again. Gulliver, still proud, privately blames the King's narrow-mindedness.

cards.q: I cannot but conclude the bulk of your natives to be the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth.
cards.b: The King of Brobdingnag's verdict on humanity, after hearing Gulliver's boasts, is the book's turning point. Seen from a giant's height, human pride shrinks. From here Gulliver's travels become darker, and his confidence in his own kind begins to crack.

Gulliver lives in a special travel box made for him by the Queen's carpenters. On a trip to the coast, a giant eagle seizes the box in its beak and carries it out over the sea, then drops it. The box floats until English sailors spot it and haul it aboard. Gulliver shouts at them as though they were giants and they were tiny, having grown so used to Brobdingnag. Back in England, he finds everything and everyone small, and his wife fears he has lost his mind. Still, he soon sets out again.

On his third voyage, attacked by pirates and set adrift, Gulliver is rescued by Laputa, a floating island held aloft by a giant magnet. Its people are obsessed with mathematics and music, so lost in thought that servants must strike them with bladders on sticks to make them speak or listen. Their clothes and houses are badly made because their theories are impractical. The King uses the island to control the land of Balnibarbi below, blocking its sunlight and rain or threatening to drop the island on rebellious towns.

In Balnibarbi's capital, Lagado, Gulliver visits the Grand Academy, a satire on the Royal Society and the scientific projects of Swift's day. Projectors labor to extract sunbeams from cucumbers, turn human excrement back into food, build houses from the roof down and soften marble for pillows. One professor has a machine that randomly combines words, hoping to write books on every subject without any learning. Meanwhile the country is in ruins, its fields barren and its people in rags, because the new methods do not work. A lord who farms in the old way is the only one prospering.

On the island of Glubbdubdrib, a sorcerer lets Gulliver summon the dead. He meets Alexander the Great, Caesar and Brutus, and discovers that history books are full of lies and that great men were often corrupt. In Luggnagg he hears of the Struldbrugs, people born immortal. Gulliver imagines what wisdom they must have, but learns the truth: they do not die, yet they keep aging, becoming miserable, forgetful, bitter and legally dead at eighty. He loses all wish to live forever. Then he sails home via Japan.

On his fourth voyage, as captain, Gulliver is put ashore by his mutinous crew. He finds a land ruled by the Houyhnhnms, noble horses who live entirely by reason. They are calm, honest, courteous and free of passion; they have no word for lying, saying only 'the thing which is not'. The land also contains Yahoos, filthy, greedy, violent humanlike creatures kept as beasts of burden. To his horror, Gulliver realizes that the Yahoos look exactly like humans. The Houyhnhnms see him as a strangely clever Yahoo.

Gulliver learns the Houyhnhnm language and lives with a master horse, explaining his country's ways. His master is baffled and disgusted by war, in which men kill each other for the sake of opinions or for kings' ambitions; by lawyers, who argue that black is white for pay; by money, which drives the rich to luxury and the poor to crime; and by doctors and politicians. The master concludes that humans have a little reason that only makes their vices worse. Gulliver, admiring the Houyhnhnms, begins to despise humanity and wants to stay forever.

The Houyhnhnms' assembly decides that Gulliver, as a Yahoo with some reason, is dangerous and must leave. Heartbroken, he builds a canoe from Yahoo skins and sails away. He is picked up by a Portuguese ship whose captain, Don Pedro de Mendez, treats him with great kindness, but Gulliver can barely stand to be near him. Back home in England, he faints when his wife kisses him, cannot bear the smell of his family, and buys two horses, talking to them for hours in the stable. He has become a misanthrope.

Gulliver is practical, curious and often naive, as his name suggests. He boasts of England to giants, admires anything powerful and adopts each new country's values. His final transformation into a man who despises humanity shows his weakness: he moves from one extreme to another, never finding a balanced view of himself or others.

cards.t: The King of Brobdingnag: the wise ruler
cards.b: The giant king embodies Swift's ideal of a ruler: practical, humane and suspicious of grand theories and violence. He prefers making two ears of corn grow where one grew before to any political scheme. His horror at gunpowder and his verdict on Europe are among the book's sharpest moral judgments.

The rational horses are honest, calm and orderly, and Gulliver worships them. Yet they have no love, passion or individuality, and they coldly debate exterminating the Yahoos. Readers argue whether Swift meant them as an ideal or a satire of pure reason. Either way, Gulliver's worship of them leads him away from humanity.

Swift uses fantasy to mock real targets: English party politics, religious wars, court corruption and the vanity of nations. By shrinking and enlarging his hero, he lets us see human customs as absurd. Pride, whether a Lilliputian emperor's or Gulliver's own, is his favorite target, and nothing escapes it.

The Laputans worship theory and ruin their country; the Academy's experiments produce nothing useful; the Houyhnhnms embody pure reason but lack compassion. Swift distrusts reason cut off from practical life and human feeling. Wisdom, in his view, lies in common sense, humility and attention to real human needs.

In Lilliput Gulliver is a giant; in Brobdingnag, a toy. The same body looks heroic or disgusting depending on the viewer. Swift shows how our judgments of beauty, power and importance depend on perspective. Seeing ourselves through others' eyes can be humbling, and it can also be distorting if we lose all sense of who we are.

cards.t: Ask which end of the egg you are fighting over
cards.b: Lilliput and Blefuscu waged war over how to crack eggs. Many disputes, in families, offices or politics, are about equally small differences. Before escalating a conflict, ask whether the issue would matter to an outsider. If not, look for a way to let it go.

cards.t: Refuse to be the tool of conquest
cards.b: Gulliver captured Blefuscu's fleet but refused to help enslave its people, and it cost him the Emperor's favor. Sometimes doing the right thing means disappointing people with power over you. When asked to use your skills to harm others, be prepared to say no, even at a cost.

cards.t: Don't boast about what you should question
cards.b: Gulliver proudly described England's wars and laws, and the King of Brobdingnag saw only corruption and cruelty. When you praise your own country, company or group, imagine an outsider's honest questions. Pride in your community is healthiest when it can survive an honest look at its faults.

The Laputans needed servants to strike them before they would notice the world, and Lagado's experiments ruined a nation. Ideas matter, but they must be tested against reality. When you start a new plan or system, ask early whether it actually helps people, and listen to those who see it failing.

cards.t: Be careful what you wish to live forever
cards.b: Gulliver imagined the Struldbrugs as wise and happy immortals, then learned they grew older and more miserable forever. Long life without health, purpose and connection is not a blessing. Focus less on how long you might live and more on how well you live each year you have.

cards.t: Don't trade humanity for an ideal
cards.b: Gulliver admired the Houyhnhnms so much that he could not stand his own family or the kind captain who saved him. Ideals can become excuses to despise real people. If your principles make you colder toward the people around you, it may be time to question the principles.

cards.t: Make two ears of corn grow
cards.b: The King of Brobdingnag valued anyone who could make two ears of corn grow where one grew before over all the politicians in the world. Practical improvements to ordinary life are worth more than grand schemes. Look for one modest, useful thing you can make better in your work or community.

Swift changed Gulliver's size to show how strange human habits look from outside. Imagine a visitor from a very different world watching your day. Which of your habits or arguments would seem as absurd to them as a war over eggs, and which would they admire?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Patient work can rebuild a life from nothing
pts.d: Crusoe learns to farm, bake, make pots and tame goats, one failed attempt at a time.

pts.h: Gratitude changes how hardship feels
pts.d: his ledger of evils and goods teaches him he has more to be thankful for than he thought.

pts.h: Restlessness can be both curse and gift
pts.d: ignoring his father's advice brings shipwreck, yet his daring also helps him survive.

pts.h: The novel reflects its age's blind spots
pts.d: Crusoe trades slaves, sells Xury and casts Friday as servant, and modern readers question this.

cards.t: A son who would go to sea
cards.b: Robinson Crusoe is born in York, England, in 1632, the son of a German merchant who settled there. His father begs him to stay in the comfortable middle station of life, free from both the poverty and the ambition that cause suffering, and warns that God will not bless him if he goes to sea. Robinson, restless, ignores him. In 1651, at nineteen, he sails from Hull without telling his parents. A terrifying storm wrecks the ship off Yarmouth, and the captain warns him never to go to sea again. Ashamed to go home, he sails on.

Crusoe makes a profitable trading voyage to the coast of Guinea in West Africa. On his second voyage, his ship is captured by Moorish pirates from Sallee, in Morocco, and he becomes the slave of their captain for two years. While out fishing, he seizes his chance: he throws his master's servant overboard and escapes in a small boat with a boy, Xury. They sail down the African coast until a Portuguese captain rescues them. Crusoe sells the boat, and also sells Xury to the captain, who promises to free him in ten years.

In Brazil, Crusoe buys land and becomes a successful sugar and tobacco planter. Wanting labor, he agrees to join a voyage to Africa to buy enslaved people for himself and his neighbors. On September 1, 1659, eight years to the day after leaving Hull, the ship sails. A hurricane drives it far off course, and it runs aground near an island off the coast of South America, near the mouth of the Orinoco River. The crew take to a boat, which a huge wave overturns. Crusoe alone is washed ashore alive, with nothing but a knife, a pipe and some tobacco.

The next morning the ship is still stuck on a rock near the shore. Over many days Crusoe swims out and builds rafts to carry off everything useful: bread, rice, cheese and rum, carpenters' tools, guns, gunpowder and shot, clothes, sails and rope, pens, ink and three Bibles. He finds a pile of coins and scornfully calls money a drug, worthless here, but takes it anyway. Then a storm breaks the ship apart. He builds a fortified home against a rock face, surrounded by a double fence of stakes, and enters it with a ladder he pulls in after him.

To track time, Crusoe carves notches into a large wooden post, marking days, Sundays and months. He keeps a journal until his ink runs out. Despairing, he writes a careful ledger of his situation in two columns, evil and good: he is cast away with no hope of rescue, but he is alive while his companions drowned; he has no clothes, but the climate is warm; he has no defense, but he has seen no wild beasts. Then, to his amazement, stalks of barley and rice sprout near his home, from grain he had shaken from an old bag.

After an earthquake and a hurricane, Crusoe falls seriously ill with fever and has a terrifying dream of a man descending from a cloud, threatening him for not repenting. In his weakness, he opens one of the Bibles and finds the words call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee. For the first time in his life, he prays sincerely. He recovers, slowly, using rum soaked with tobacco as a remedy, and begins to see his island as a place of deliverance rather than only a prison. He reads the Bible daily.

Over the years, Crusoe becomes skilled at almost everything. He explores the island, finds grapes, melons and limes, and builds a country bower. He domesticates wild goats for milk, meat and cheese, grows and harvests grain, and teaches himself to make pottery, baskets, bread and clothes of goatskin, with an umbrella. He tames a parrot, Poll, who calls his name. He spends months building a huge canoe, only to find it too heavy to move to the sea. A smaller canoe nearly carries him away on a powerful current.

After about fifteen years alone, Crusoe walks along the shore one day and stops dead. There, clearly visible in the sand, is the print of a single bare human foot. He rushes back to his fortress in terror, looking behind him at every step, imagining devils and savages. For days he cannot sleep. He strengthens his fortifications, plants groves of trees to hide his home, and divides his goats among several pens in case enemies find them. The footprint shatters the peace he has built and shows him how fear can overwhelm faith.

cards.q: It happened one day, about noon, going towards my boat, I was exceedingly surprised with the print of a man's naked foot on the shore, which was very plain to be seen in the sand.
cards.b: Defoe's most famous sentence marks the novel's turning point. After years of solitary mastery, Crusoe learns he is not alone, and his story turns from survival against nature to encounters with other people, full of fear, violence and eventual companionship.

Some time later, Crusoe finds the shore on the far side of the island littered with skulls, hands, feet and other bones around the remains of a fire: cannibals from the mainland have been holding feasts there. He is horrified and spends years living cautiously, avoiding fires that might give him away. He thinks about attacking the cannibals, but reflects that they are not acting from malice and that God has not appointed him their judge. Years later, he sees the wreck of a Spanish ship nearby, but no survivors. He longs desperately for human company.

In his twenty-fifth year on the island, Crusoe watches cannibals land with two prisoners. One is killed; the other breaks free and runs toward him, pursued by two men. Crusoe knocks one down and shoots the other. The rescued man kneels and places Crusoe's foot on his head as a sign of submission. Crusoe names him Friday, after the day they met. He teaches Friday English, to eat goat instead of human flesh, and Christianity, while Friday asks searching questions about God and the devil. Crusoe calls him his servant, but grows to love him.

When cannibals arrive with more prisoners, Crusoe and Friday attack, freeing a Spaniard and an old man who turns out to be Friday's father. Crusoe sends them to the mainland to fetch other shipwrecked Spaniards. Before they return, an English ship anchors offshore: its crew has mutinied and is about to maroon the captain. Crusoe and Friday free the captain and, with cunning and bluff, Crusoe pretending to be the island's governor, help him overpower the mutineers and retake the ship. The worst of the rebels are left behind on the island.

Crusoe leaves the island on December 19, 1686, after twenty-eight years, two months and nineteen days, taking Friday, his goatskin cap, umbrella and parrot. In England, he finds his parents dead. He learns that his Brazilian plantation has prospered and made him rich, thanks to honest partners. Traveling overland through the Pyrenees, he and Friday fight off a pack of hungry wolves and a bear. Crusoe marries and has children, and after his wife dies, he revisits his island, now a small colony, ready for further adventures.

Crusoe is restless, stubborn and self-reliant, a methodical man who counts, measures and records everything. He turns a desert island into a farm, fortress and kingdom. Defoe presents him as a kind of everyman of the new commercial age: resourceful and religious, but also a slave trader and a self-styled monarch who sees ownership everywhere.

Friday is loyal, quick and affectionate, and his questions about God expose gaps in Crusoe's faith. But he is defined through Crusoe's eyes, named, renamed and taught to call Crusoe 'Master'. Modern readers see in their relationship the patterns of colonialism, and many retellings give Friday his own voice.

cards.t: Crusoe's father: the voice of caution
cards.b: Crusoe's father appears only at the start, but his advice echoes throughout. He praises the safe, modest middle station of life and warns that his son will regret ignoring it. Crusoe's island suffering partly fulfills that warning, yet his adventures also bring wealth, faith and growth his father never imagined.

Much of the novel is a detailed record of work: building, farming, baking, potting and sewing. Defoe celebrates ingenuity and persistence, showing how one man with tools and patience can create civilization. Crusoe's many failed attempts, at pots and canoes, are as instructive as his successes.

Crusoe interprets his shipwreck as punishment for disobedience and his survival as divine mercy. His conversion during illness transforms his solitude into a spiritual retreat. Defoe, a devout Dissenter, frames the adventure as a spiritual autobiography, in which every event can be read as a sign of God's care.

Crusoe calls the island his kingdom, names Friday, and later governs Spanish and English settlers. He was shipwrecked on a slaving voyage and sold Xury for money. Defoe's novel, written at the height of Britain's colonial expansion, reflects its assumptions of European mastery, and today's readers examine these themes critically.

cards.t: Make a ledger of good and evil
cards.b: Crusoe's two-column list showed him that, for every misfortune, he had something to be grateful for. When you feel overwhelmed, try writing your own: the hard things on one side, the blessings and resources on the other. You may find more on the second side than you expected.

cards.t: Save what you can from the wreck
cards.b: Before the ship broke apart, Crusoe made trip after trip to carry off every useful thing. After a setback, a lost job, a broken plan, ask what you can still salvage: skills, contacts, lessons, a few tools. Rebuilding is easier when you start with what survived.

Crusoe's first pots cracked, his great canoe never reached the water, and his first harvests failed. Each failure taught him something. When a project goes wrong, examine why, adjust and try again. Mastery often comes from a long series of imperfect attempts, not from getting it right the first time.

cards.t: Measure the boat before you build it
cards.b: Crusoe spent months carving a huge canoe and only then realized he could not move it to the sea. Enthusiasm can blind us to practical limits. Before investing heavily in a project, check that you can actually finish it and get it to where it needs to go.

cards.t: Don't let one footprint undo your peace
cards.b: A single footprint sent Crusoe into years of fear after he had built a secure life. Sudden threats can make us forget our resources and resilience. When fear strikes, take sensible precautions, but remind yourself of what you have already survived and built.

cards.t: Notice when you treat people as property
cards.b: Crusoe sold Xury and called Friday his servant, though both had saved or served him faithfully. It is easy to see the injustices of other centuries clearly and miss our own. Ask whether you ever treat people mainly as useful to you, and how you might honor their dignity instead.

Crusoe notched a post every day so he would not lose track of time, Sundays and himself. Simple routines and records anchor us in hard periods. In times of isolation or chaos, keep a few steady habits, a journal, a daily walk, a weekly call, to remember who you are.

Crusoe discovered he could make bread, pots, clothes and a home with his own hands, after years of failures. If you were cut off from everything you rely on, what skills would you wish you had? Is there one you could start learning now?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Meddling in others' lives often backfires
pts.d: Emma's matchmaking breaks Harriet's heart twice and nearly costs her a good husband.

pts.h: Cleverness can blind us to the obvious
pts.d: Emma reads everyone's hearts wrongly, including her own love for Mr. Knightley.

pts.h: Privilege carries a duty of kindness
pts.d: Emma's careless joke at poor Miss Bates at Box Hill is the novel's moral crisis.

pts.h: True friends tell us hard truths
pts.d: Mr. Knightley's rebukes, not flattery, are what help Emma grow.

cards.b: Emma Woodhouse, almost twenty-one, lives at Hartfield, the finest house in the village of Highbury in Surrey, in the early 1800s. She is handsome, clever and rich, and has had very little to distress her. She keeps house for her kindly, fussy, hypochondriac father, Mr. Woodhouse, who hates change and worries about drafts and rich food. As the story opens, Emma's beloved governess, Miss Taylor, has just married their neighbor Mr. Weston. Emma claims credit for the match and decides that matchmaking is her talent, despite the warnings of their old friend, Mr. Knightley.

Mr. Knightley, about thirty-seven, is the sensible, generous owner of the nearby Donwell Abbey estate and the brother of Emma's sister Isabella's husband. He is the only person who ever criticizes Emma. Emma befriends Harriet Smith, a pretty, sweet, rather simple seventeen-year-old of unknown parentage who boards at the local school. Harriet is fond of Robert Martin, a respectable young farmer who rents land from Mr. Knightley. When Robert writes to propose, Emma persuades Harriet that he is beneath her, and Harriet refuses him. Knightley is furious with Emma for spoiling a good match.

Emma has chosen a husband for Harriet: the handsome young vicar, Mr. Elton. She draws Harriet's portrait, and Elton praises it extravagantly and offers to have it framed in London. He gives them a charade, a riddle whose answer is 'courtship', which Emma is sure is addressed to Harriet. Knightley warns Emma that Elton is ambitious and will never marry a girl with no fortune or family. Emma ignores him. She believes she understands everyone's heart perfectly, and she encourages Harriet's hopes.

After a Christmas Eve party at the Westons', Emma finds herself alone in a carriage with Mr. Elton, who has drunk too much wine. To her horror, he declares passionate love for her, not Harriet; all his attentions were meant for Emma. When she tells him he was supposed to love Harriet, he is insulted at the idea. Emma refuses him coldly. Then she must break the news to Harriet, who is devastated. Elton goes off to Bath and returns weeks later engaged to a rich, vulgar, self-important woman, Augusta Hawkins.

Two long-awaited visitors arrive. Frank Churchill, Mr. Weston's son, raised by rich relatives, is handsome, lively and charming, and he flirts with Emma, who enjoys it while deciding she will not fall in love. Jane Fairfax, the orphaned niece of the poor, talkative spinster Miss Bates, is elegant and talented but reserved, and Emma, a little jealous, dislikes her. When a piano arrives for Jane as an anonymous gift, Emma speculates to Frank that it came from a married man, Mr. Dixon. Knightley suspects something between Frank and Jane.

At a ball at the Crown Inn, Mr. Elton pointedly refuses to dance with Harriet, humiliating her, and Mr. Knightley, who never dances, steps in and asks her himself. The next day, Harriet is cornered by gypsy children demanding money, and Frank Churchill rescues her. Later, Harriet tells Emma she has fallen in love with someone far above her, after a great service he did her. Emma assumes she means Frank and the rescue, and quietly encourages her, without naming names. It is another misunderstanding.

Mr. Knightley hosts a strawberry-picking party at Donwell Abbey. Mrs. Elton, now the village's self-appointed leader, patronizes everyone, especially Jane, whom she pushes to accept a position as a governess, a job Jane dreads. Jane slips away early, upset. Frank arrives late and in a bad temper, complaining of the heat. Emma notices little, while Knightley, watching Frank and Jane, grows more suspicious. Mr. Woodhouse, meanwhile, frets about everyone's health. Austen fills Highbury's everyday events with clues the reader, like Emma, may miss.

The next day a party goes on an outing to Box Hill, a famous beauty spot. Everyone is bored and out of sorts. Frank flirts with Emma loudly and proposes a game: each person must say one very clever thing, two moderately clever things, or three very dull ones. Kind, chattering Miss Bates laughs that she will certainly say three dull things. Emma cannot resist: she remarks that Miss Bates may find it difficult to limit herself to only three. Miss Bates understands, blushes and is hurt.

cards.q: How could you be so unfeeling to Miss Bates? How could you be so insolent in your wit to a woman of her character, age, and situation?
cards.b: Mr. Knightley's words to Emma as the party leaves Box Hill are the novel's turning point. He reminds her that Miss Bates is poor, aging and has known Emma since infancy. Emma, who has always been praised, feels true shame for the first time, and she weeps all the way home.

The next morning Emma visits Miss Bates to make amends, warmly and humbly. Jane, now ill, refuses to see her. Then news spreads that Frank's demanding aunt, Mrs. Churchill, has died. Soon Mr. and Mrs. Weston reveal an astonishing secret: Frank and Jane have been secretly engaged since meeting at the seaside resort of Weymouth months earlier. Frank's flirtation with Emma was a cover. Jane's misery and illness came from guilt and jealousy. Emma is shocked to realize how much she misread, and how Frank used her.

Emma worries about Harriet's feelings for Frank. But Harriet explains that she never meant Frank. The man she loves is Mr. Knightley, who rescued her from humiliation at the ball, and she believes he may return her feelings. As Emma hears this, a sudden realization strikes her like an arrow: Mr. Knightley must marry no one but herself. She has loved him all along. Now she fears that her own encouragement has given Harriet hopes that could cost Emma the man she loves, and she sees her vanity clearly.

Mr. Knightley returns from London, believing Emma is heartbroken over Frank. Walking in the garden at Hartfield, he tries to comfort her, and Emma assures him she never loved Frank. Hesitantly, Knightley declares that he has loved her for years, and asks if she can return his feelings. She can. There is one problem: Mr. Woodhouse cannot bear to lose Emma or change his routines. Knightley generously agrees to move into Hartfield after the wedding so she need not leave her father.

Emma dreads telling Harriet, but Harriet, sent to London, meets Robert Martin again, and he proposes once more. This time she accepts happily. Harriet's father turns out to be a respectable tradesman, not the gentleman Emma had imagined. Mr. Woodhouse still resists the marriage, until a series of poultry thefts in the neighborhood frightens him into wanting a man in the house. Emma and Mr. Knightley marry in a small, simple ceremony. Frank and Jane will marry, and Harriet and Robert Martin find their own happiness.

Austen said she was writing a heroine whom no one but herself would much like. Emma is snobbish, vain and meddling, yet also warm, witty, loyal and generous to her father. Her charm is that she can be wrong, admit it and grow. The novel is the story of a clever young woman learning to see clearly.

Mr. Knightley is sensible, kind and direct. He values character over rank, respects Robert Martin and shows tenderness to Miss Bates and Harriet. He is the only one who tells Emma the truth, even when it hurts her. Austen makes him the novel's moral compass and Emma's ideal partner.

cards.t: Miss Bates: the comic and the vulnerable
cards.b: Miss Bates talks endlessly about trivial things and is easy to laugh at. Yet she is unfailingly kind, grateful and humble, living in genteel poverty with her aged mother. Austen uses her to test the other characters: how they treat Miss Bates reveals who they truly are, as Emma learns at Box Hill.

Emma is sure she can read everyone, yet she misjudges Elton, Frank, Jane, Harriet and her own heart. Austen fills the novel with clues, riddles and misunderstandings, making readers share Emma's blindness. The book is a study of how confidence and imagination can mislead us, and how self-knowledge comes through humility.

Highbury is a world of fine distinctions between gentry, farmers and tradespeople. Emma's snobbery leads her to reject Robert Martin for Harriet, while Mrs. Elton's vulgar pretensions mock social climbing. Austen suggests that rank brings responsibilities, and that worth lies in character and kindness, not in fortune or family.

Highbury's dinners, balls, picnics and gossip form the whole world of the novel. Austen shows that ordinary village life is full of drama, moral choices and comedy. In such a small community, words and actions travel fast, and a single careless remark can wound deeply and be remembered.

cards.t: Let people choose their own path
cards.b: Emma persuaded Harriet to refuse Robert Martin, a man she loved, because he did not fit Emma's plan. It took heartbreak to undo the damage. When you are tempted to steer a friend's choices in love, work or life, offer support and honesty, but let them decide.

Emma assumed Elton's riddle was for Harriet and that Harriet loved Frank; both were wrong. When you think you know what someone means or wants, ask them directly. Many misunderstandings come from confidently filling in gaps that a simple question could have answered.

cards.t: Wit is no excuse for cruelty
cards.b: Emma's joke at Miss Bates was clever, and it cut a kind, poor woman in front of everyone. A sharp remark can wound long after the laugh fades. Before making a joke at someone's expense, especially someone with less power or status, ask whether it is worth the hurt.

The morning after Box Hill, Emma visited Miss Bates and treated her with warmth and respect. It did not erase the insult, but it began the repair. When you have hurt someone, do not wait for the perfect moment. Go soon, in person if possible, and show through actions that you understand.

cards.t: Value the friend who corrects you
cards.b: Mr. Knightley was the only person who ever told Emma she was wrong, and that is why she came to love and respect him. Flattery is pleasant; honest criticism helps us grow. Notice who in your life tells you hard truths kindly, and treasure them.

Frank Churchill hid his engagement by flirting with Emma, causing confusion and pain to Jane, Emma and others. Keeping secrets may sometimes be necessary, but using other people as a cover is unfair. If you must keep something private, make sure others do not pay the price.

cards.t: Look closer to home for love
cards.b: Emma searched everywhere for matches while the man she loved was in her drawing room every week. Sometimes what we most need is right in front of us, in a long friendship or familiar relationship. Take time to notice the people who are already steadily present in your life.

Emma was sure she understood everyone in Highbury and was wrong about almost all of them. Who in your life might you have misjudged, too quickly or too confidently? What question could you ask them that would help you see them more clearly?
